title: Book language and street language
goal: Understand why the Persian you read and the Persian you hear sound like two languages — and master the ten rules that turn one into the other.
bekal: turn written sentences into spoken ones and back
understand everyday conversation, TV series, and taxi drivers

dialogs.title: گفتگو — چرا هیچی نمی‌فهمم؟

notes: **Most of the rules are sensible shortcuts.** The mouth cuts whatever it can: می‌روم (three syllables) becomes می‌رم (two), است becomes a single sound ـه, and برای becomes واسه. If you say the spoken form while noticing where it came from, you'll remember it much faster than by memorizing a list.
**Maryam's line** دهان تنبل‌تر از قلم است is worth remembering. Every language in the world does the same thing; Persian is just more open about it.
**The verb حرف زدن = "to talk"**, literally "to strike words". In conversation it's used more than صحبت کردن. Spoken حرف می‌زنم → *harf mizanam* (unchanged), but the شما form is حرف می‌زنین.

**The phrase فرق داشتن = "to be different"**, from فرق ("difference") — an Arabic loan from the root ف-ر-ق, "to separate" (the same root as *Furqan*). این با آن فرق دارد = "this is different from that".

⚠️ **Which one should you use?** For **speaking** — the spoken form; it sounds natural and friendly. For **formal messages, letters, or exams** — the written form. Using the written form in conversation isn't wrong or rude; it just sounds very polite and a bit stiff, like someone speaking in perfect textbook English at a corner café.

**The way to learn this is not by memorizing a table.** Read every dialog in this module once more, and each time turn it into the spoken form in your head. After five units, the changes become automatic. That's why this unit sits in the middle of the module and not at the end.

grammars.title: Ten rules that turn written into spoken
after: **Rule 6 claims the most victims**, because it hits the most common verbs. Memorize these six and you've mastered half of Iranian conversation:
می‌روم → **می‌رم** · می‌شوم → **می‌شم** · می‌گویم → **می‌گم** · می‌دهم → **می‌دم** · می‌خواهم → **می‌خوام** · می‌آیم → **میام**
And two verbs that join rule 2: می‌دانم → **می‌دونم** (*midunam*), می‌توانم → **می‌تونم** (*mitunam*).

grammars.title: Same sentence, two faces
after: Look at the sixth row: in the spoken form, **the verb isn't always at the end of the sentence anymore**. من می‌رم خونه puts the destination after the verb. This freedom only applies in conversation; in writing, the verb stays at the end.

grammars.title: Words that change completely in conversation
after: **The word دیگه is the one you'll hear most and the hardest to translate.** It adds a tone of "come on", "you know", "well" to a sentence: بریم دیگه! ("come on, let's go!"), همینه دیگه ("that's just how it is"). English does something similar with "you know" and "come on".

**Two casual terms, داداش ("bro") and آبجی ("sis"),** are friendly ways to address strangers your own age — taxi drivers, shopkeepers, waiters. Warm, but only between people of similar age; with older people, stick to آقا and خانم.

sections.title: Listening practice: what you'll actually hear

blocks.text: These ten phrases are what you'll hear most on the streets of Tehran in your first ten minutes. You've learned all of them — in their written form.
⚠️ **Spoken یه = یک.** The number one is almost never said in full in conversation: یه چای ("a tea"), یه لحظه ("a moment"), یه کم ("a little"). This is the eleventh rule that didn't fit in the table.

blocks.title: A phrase that sounds terrifying but means something sweet: قربونت
items: Literally, قربانت (*ghorbânet*) means "may I be your sacrifice" — and all it means is "thanks so much" or "love you". Its relatives قربونت برم ("may I become your sacrifice") and فدات شم ("may I be your ransom") are both used with loved ones, especially children and close friends.
Persian is full of affectionate expressions that are shockingly over-the-top when taken literally. Don't translate them word for word; translate the **tone**, not the words.

blocks.title: Three ways to train your ear starting tonight
items: **Watch anything from Iran with Persian subtitles.** Your eyes read the written form, your ears hear the spoken form, and your brain pairs them up on its own. It's the most efficient way to learn there is.
**Turn one dialog from this module into the spoken form every day.** Write two columns in your notebook: written on the left, spoken on the right. Ten minutes, twenty days, done.
**Listen to Persian songs and read the lyrics.** Songs mix both forms, so your ear learns to switch back and forth — exactly what real conversation demands.
